name: Norwegian Bokmål (Urban East Norwegian)
variety: Urban East Norwegian, the educated speech of Oslo and the surrounding region, the usual spoken form of Bokmål and the variety described by Kristoffersen (2000)
sources: Kristoffersen, Gjert (2000). The Phonology of Norwegian. Oxford University Press.
Vanvik, Arne (1979). Norsk fonetikk. Oslo: Universitetet i Oslo.
Haugen, Einar and Joos, Martin (1952). Tone and intonation in East Norwegian. Acta Philologica Scandinavica 22, 41-64.
Fintoft, Knut (1970). Acoustical Analysis and Perception of Tonemes in Some Norwegian Dialects. Oslo: Universitetsforlaget.
Fretheim, Thorstein and Nilsen, Randi Alice (1989). Terminal rise and rise-fall tunes in East Norwegian intonation. Nordic Journal of Linguistics 12, 155-181.
Simonsen, Hanne Gram; Moen, Inger; Cowen, Steve (2008). Norwegian retroflex stops in a cross linguistic perspective. Journal of Phonetics 36, 385-405.
Ringen, Catherine and van Dommelen, Wim A. (2013). Quantity and laryngeal contrasts in Norwegian. Journal of Phonetics 41, 479-490.
contrasts: two word accents on stressed syllables of words with at least one following syllable: accent 1 bønder 'farmers' versus accent 2 bønner 'beans', accent 1 loven 'the law' versus accent 2 låven 'the barn', accent 1 tanken 'the tank' versus accent 2 tanken 'the thought'
complementary quantity in stressed syllables: long vowel plus short consonant versus short vowel plus long consonant (tak [tɑːk] 'roof' versus takk [tɑkː] 'thanks', hat versus hatt)
three close rounded vowels /y ʉ u/ with different lip rounding and tongue position (by, bu, bo)
nine vowel qualities, each long and short
dental or alveolar /t d n l s/ versus retroflex /ʈ ɖ ɳ ɭ ʂ/ (kart [kɑʈ] versus katt)
/ç/ versus /ʂ/ (kjede versus skjede), a contrast that many younger speakers have merged
allophony: /ɾ/ plus a following /t d n l s/ fuse to retroflex [ʈ ɖ ɳ ɭ ʂ], inside words and across word boundaries (barn [bɑːɳ], norsk [nɔʂk], vær så god with [ʂ]); the retroflexion spreads through a cluster (barnslig)
written rd is [ɾ] in many common words (bord [buːɾ], gård) and [ɖ] in others (ferdig [ˈfæɖɪ])
/ɾ/ is a tap; the retroflex flap [ɽ] ('thick l') replaces /l/ after some vowels and written rd in informal speech (sol, blå, gård)
/p t k/ are aspirated at the start of a stressed syllable and unaspirated after /s/; /b d ɡ/ are unaspirated and only partly voiced
/e/ and /eː/ are lowered to [æ æː] before /ɾ/ and the retroflexes (her [hæːɾ], ferdig, verden)
/ʂ/ comes from sj, skj, sk before front vowels and from rs; /ç/ from kj, tj and k before front vowels; /ç/ is often alveolo-palatal [ɕ]
/t d n l/ are laminal dental or alveolar, the retroflexes are apical postalveolar
long vowels may end in a slight centring offglide; long /iː yː/ may end in friction
unstressed e is schwa; -er is [əɾ] and -en [ən] or a syllabic [n̩]
nd and ld are [n] and [l] with length after a short vowel (land [lɑnː], kveld)
h in hj and hv, g in gj, and d after a long vowel at the end of many words are silent (hjem, hva, god [ɡuː], rød)
phonotactics: a stressed syllable is heavy: it has a long vowel, a diphthong, or a short vowel followed by a long consonant or a cluster
unstressed syllables have short vowels and short consonants
onset clusters of up to three consonants, the first being /s/ (spr, str, skr)
retroflex consonants do not begin native words, and /ŋ/ never begins a word
accent 2 needs at least one syllable after the stressed one; monosyllables and words with final stress have accent 1

stress.type: lexical, mostly initial in native words
stress.rule: Native words stress the first syllable of the stem, the prefixes be- and for- are unstressed, compounds stress their first member, and loans from French, Latin and Greek stress the last or second-last syllable (stasjon, universitet, banan, student).
stress.cues: the tonal accent, which only stressed syllables carry, together with the length of the vowel or of the consonant after it; intensity is secondary

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: unstressed e is schwa and unstressed vowels are short, but other unstressed vowels keep their quality
rhythm.notes: I know of no published nPVI value for Urban East Norwegian.

length.notes: Length is complementary in stressed syllables: a long vowel is followed by a short consonant and a short vowel by a long consonant or a cluster. Unstressed syllables have no length contrast. I cannot quote duration ratios with confidence.

intonation.declarative: the utterance is a chain of accent phrases; each starts with the word accent of its stressed syllable and ends in a rise to a high tone, and the rise is largest in the focused phrase; after the last high tone the pitch falls slightly or stays high, so that statements can sound rising to speakers of other languages
intonation.yes_no_question: the same chain of accent phrases with a higher final rise; questions with inversion need no special tune
intonation.wh_question: as in statements, with the largest rise on the focused phrase and a low or slightly falling end
intonation.continuation: the high end of the last accent phrase is kept, without a fall
intonation.accent_shape: accent 1 is L*H: low in the stressed syllable, then a rise to the end of the accent phrase; accent 2 is H*LH: high at the start of the stressed syllable, a fall to low late in that syllable or in the next, then a rise to the end of the accent phrase
intonation.notes: East Norwegian is a 'low-tone' dialect: the stressed syllable of accent 1 is low. West and North Norwegian dialects are 'high-tone' dialects with the reverse timing. Analysis after Kristoffersen (2000) and Fretheim and Nilsen (1989).

inventory.name: accent 1
inventory.description: low level or slightly falling pitch in the stressed syllable, then a rise that reaches its peak at the end of the accent phrase (in a word of two syllables said alone, on the second syllable)

inventory.name: accent 2
inventory.description: high pitch at the start of the stressed syllable, falling to low by the end of that syllable or the start of the next, then a rise that reaches its peak at the end of the accent phrase

sandhi: the accent belongs to the stressed syllable; the following unstressed syllables, also those of following unstressed words, carry the rest of the contour up to the next stressed syllable
compounds have one accent, decided by the first member
without focus the final rise of the accent phrase is small; under focus it is large
tone.neutral_tone: unstressed syllables have no accent of their own and continue the contour of the accent phrase; syllables before the first stress are low to mid
tone.notes: The Chao numerals are a schematic rendering of the citation form of a word of two syllables, not measured values. eSpeak NG has no tone phonemes for Norwegian, so the espeak field is empty.

phonation: aspiration of /p t k/; no contrastive voice quality

problems: the word accents are not marked anywhere: the phoneme table has no tone phonemes and the dictionary has no accent marks, so bønder and bønner, and the two words tanken, sound the same
retroflexes are missing: rt, rd, rn, rl are said as r plus a dental ([kʊrt], [bɑrn], [parla]); only rs is changed, to the postalveolar [ʃ]; nothing happens across word boundaries
kj and k before front vowels are the velar fricative [x], not the palatal [ç], while tj is an alveolo-palatal sibilant: one phoneme has two wrong renderings

stressed a before a single consonant is short and front (dag, mat, tak, sak, gate come out with the short phoneme a, which is the one the table uses for /æ/) where the language has long [ɑː]; tak and takk therefore differ in the wrong way
the letter o is [uː] by default, so words with [oː] or [ɔ] are wrong unless a rule catches them (loven comes out with [uː])
every word is stressed on its first syllable: stasjon, universitet, telefon, banan, student
silent letters are pronounced: god is [ɡuːd], og is [uːɡ]; the dictionary has about 240 entries and the rule file only a handful of rules for each letter
final unstressed -e is an open schwa [a]-like vowel (phoneme a#) where the language has [ə]
r is a trill, where the language has a tap
questions are given the same tune whether they are yes-no or wh-questions
good: long and short vowels are separate phonemes with their own length, and double consonant letters give long consonants (takk [tɑkː], hatt)
the three close rounded vowels [y ʉ u] are kept apart
nd and ld are assimilated (land, hund)
the voice uses intonation group 4, in which statements end in a rise; this suits the high end of East Norwegian accent phrases, although only at the end of the clause

notes: In the consonant list the retroflexes arise mostly from /ɾ/ plus a dental, and /ɽ/ belongs to informal speech. In the diphthong list ɔʏ, ɑɪ and ʉɪ are marginal (loans and a few words). I give no formant, voice onset time or duration values because I cannot quote published figures for this variety with confidence.
